text: At real scale, the honest answer to 'what services do we run, and who owns each one' is usually a stale wiki page or 'ask around in Slack.' That's not a documentation gap, it's a missing source of truth, and it's the first thing a developer self-service portal has to fix before a golden path means anything.

A software catalog represents every component as a structured entity -- a Component, an API, a Resource, a System, a Group, or a User. Each one carries a real owner, like a specific team rather than a name nobody can reach, a lifecycle stage, and a dependsOn list that builds an org-wide dependency graph automatically, instead of someone drawing it by hand and letting it go stale.

In Backstage, the reference implementation of this idea, that entity is a catalog-info.yaml committed right alongside the service's own code. Declare kind Component, fill in owner and lifecycle, and that one file is what makes checkout-service real to the catalog -- searchable, owned, and connected to whatever it depends on. If the file goes missing or the owner field is wrong, that's immediately visible, not silently rotting.

Knowing what exists is half the problem. The other half is how new things get created. A software template -- Backstage calls it the Scaffolder -- is a self-service wizard backed by a template.yaml. A developer fills out a short form, and three steps run in order: fetch a skeleton source tree, publish it as a real repository, then register that new component in the catalog automatically, closing the loop between creation and inventory.

That's what separates a golden-path template from copy-pasting an existing repo and stripping out the business logic. The generated service already has its CI/CD pipeline wired, a monitoring dashboard included rather than bolted on weeks later, and infrastructure connected -- and because the template calls catalog colon register, it's visible org-wide the moment it's created, with a real owner already attached.

The catalog and the templates depend on each other: a catalog is only trustworthy if new services reliably show up in it, and a template that never registers its output just creates more invisible sprawl. Next lesson looks at the whole portal built on top of that trustworthy data -- what a Backstage-style developer portal actually provides beyond a wiki.
